#454 — the two things that make this case HERMETIC, both of which it previously only appeared to be. (1) Its own fixture, `fx-merged-extends-child`, rather than the differential sibling's `fx-tier1-extends-child`. That fixture declares `ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/node:1`, and `--include-merged-configuration` RESOLVES the feature set to fold each feature's metadata into the merged document — a ghcr.io fetch whose failure is fatal (correctly: a declared feature that cannot be fetched must fail fast). Watched to fail: with the network namespace removed, this case exited 1 with `Failed to fetch feature 'ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/node:1'` — the exact `chan-exit-code: Diverge; chan-structured-output: Diverge` signature the flake reported. The new fixture declares a LOCAL feature instead, which needs no registry and still exercises the feature-metadata contribution to `mergedConfiguration`. (2) `--docker-path` naming a binary that does not exist. A merged read on an image-shaped config inspects the base image's `devcontainer.metadata` LABEL and PULLS on a cache miss (#307) — so on any runner with a daemon this case downloaded `mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/base:bookworm` (1.2 GB) inside the lane that gates every pull request, and a registry that HANGS rather than fails would take the whole run to CASE_TIMEOUT. The flag removes that reach and turns it into an assertion: `--include-merged-configuration` must degrade cleanly when no container runtime exists, which nothing else pins. It also makes the case SUBSTRATE-INDEPENDENT — before, the merged document silently gained the base image's baked `customizations` on machines that happened to have the image cached and not on machines that did not. Neither the exit code nor the `image` signal depends on either reach: `mergedConfiguration.image` is echoed from the parent document, which is precisely what this case claims. Measured after the change: exit 0 in 165 ms with the network namespace removed, byte-identical to the run with network and a real daemon. The reaches are NOT gratuitous product behavior and are not being worked around — they stay covered by the Docker-lane and differential merged cases, whose jobs provision for them.

FR-040 boundary class: every collection-valued field is present and EMPTY — `features`, `forwardPorts`, `containerEnv`, `remoteEnv`, `mounts`, `runArgs`, `customizations`. An empty collection is the edge of the accepted domain and is distinct from an omitted field, which is exactly the distinction the `null_preserving` rule exists to keep visible. STRENGTHENED BY #398, which is what made the strengthening possible: until deacon wrapped the eleven bare-collection properties in `Option`, it emitted these keys whether or not the author wrote them, `drop_absent_optional` elided them from deacon's side, and observing `chan-structured-output` here would have compared a document with the fields removed — the case would have been green while proving nothing about the very boundary it names. deacon now emits exactly the authored eight and the rule no longer touches this block, so the channel is added and the boundary is actually compared. Measured at oracle 0.87.0: both CLIs emit the same ten keys, with no tolerance.

Closes `config-source=compose` x `features=multiple-dependency-order`. The Compose counterpart of `case-readconfig-overlay-dockerfile-depends`: the configuration declares only `needs-base-tool`, and `base-tool` — which it `installsAfter` — arrives ONLY through `--additional-features`, so dependency order has to be decided across the configuration and the overlay together. Positional for the same reason as its Dockerfile sibling. Its existence is the pairwise question stated plainly: the Dockerfile case proves nothing about whether a Compose-shaped configuration resolves the same way, which is why the pair was counted as a hole rather than assumed covered.

Closes `features=lockfile` x `layering=image-metadata`, the last pair reachable only through the merged document. The merged configuration for a Compose project layers the pinned Feature's own metadata onto the authored configuration, and the assertion names the Compose identity (`service`, `workspaceFolder`) beside the Feature pin so a merge that resolved the Feature while losing the service binding could not pass. The Feature's contributed `customizations` are deliberately NOT asserted: they are the FEATURE's published content, they change when the pinned version's metadata changes upstream, and a case whose verdict moved with that would be measuring the Feature rather than the merge. Relabelled from `features=lockfile` to `single`: this case asserts Feature keys that come from `devcontainer.json`, and `read-configuration` never consults a lockfile at all, so nothing here could distinguish one being present from one being absent. The fixture declares exactly one Feature, which is what `single` names. See `rule-no-lockfile-for-configuration-reporting`.

Closes three pairs at once — `config-source=compose` x `features=lockfile`, `config-source=compose` x `layering=cli-overlay`, and `features=lockfile` x `layering=cli-overlay`. A Compose project whose Feature is pinned by a committed `devcontainer-lock.json`, read through a merge-fragment overlay. The assertion keeps the pinned Feature id alongside the overlaid `name`: an overlay that silently dropped the Feature set while applying its own keys would pass an assertion naming only the overlaid value, and dropping Features is exactly the failure a Compose-plus-lockfile read invites. Reading reports the DECLARED Feature set — consuming the lockfile belongs to `upgrade` and `up` — so the case makes the combination reachable without claiming the read resolves the pin. Relabelled from `features=lockfile` to `single`: this case asserts Feature keys that come from `devcontainer.json`, and `read-configuration` never consults a lockfile at all, so nothing here could distinguish one being present from one being absent. The fixture declares exactly one Feature, which is what `single` names. See `rule-no-lockfile-for-configuration-reporting`.

Closes `features=single` x `layering=cli-overlay`. One Feature, one merge fragment: the fragment renames the configuration and the single declared Feature survives untouched. The pairing matters because a merge fragment and a Feature set are the two things an overlay can most easily get wrong together — replacing the base wholesale would drop the Feature, and deep-merging the `features` map wrongly would duplicate it — so the assertion names both the overlaid `name` and the surviving Feature id rather than either alone. It also carries the hermetic guard for #439's reported Feature shape: `id` is the Feature's OWN id (deacon reported the canonical `local:<absolute path>` before, leaking a host path into an identity field), plus `version`/`name` from the Feature's metadata, the constant `internalVersion`, and the install-order `consecutiveId`. The differential lane covers this shape too, but only with a live oracle; this case fails on a plain `dev-fast` run.

Closes `config-source=dockerfile` x `features=multiple-declared-order` and `features=multiple-declared-order` x `layering=cli-overlay`. Two local Features with no dependency between them, so the order is DECLARED rather than derived: `overrideFeatureInstallOrder` names `beta-tool` first while the `features` map lists `alpha-tool` first, and the resolved order must follow the override. The array assertion is positional for the reason `case-readconfig-overlay-dockerfile-depends` records — a `jsonSubset` over an array matches without regard to order, so a non-positional assertion would pass for an implementation that ignored the override entirely. The overlay is a merge fragment rather than `--additional-features` so the declared order stays two Features long and the case measures ordering, not arrival.

Closes `config-source=dockerfile` x `features=lockfile` and `features=lockfile` x `layering=extends-chain`. The child document carries nothing but `extends` and a `name`; the Dockerfile build, the version-pinned Feature and `remoteUser` all reach the merged result through the base. Asserting all four together is the point — a chain that resolved the child's own keys but dropped the base's `features` would satisfy an assertion naming only `name`, and that is the failure mode an extends chain carrying a pinned Feature actually has. `--include-merged-configuration` is required because a plain read ECHOES `extends` rather than resolving it, which is deacon's characterized behavior, not an accident of this fixture. Relabelled from `features=lockfile` to `single`: this case asserts Feature keys that come from `devcontainer.json`, and `read-configuration` never consults a lockfile at all, so nothing here could distinguish one being present from one being absent. The fixture declares exactly one Feature, which is what `single` names. See `rule-no-lockfile-for-configuration-reporting`.

The hermetic half of #430. deacon rejected this document until 2026-08-03 — `features` declaring one Feature at two versions — and the spec says all three of the things that made the rejection wrong: `feature-dependencies.md` §Definition: Feature Equality makes OCI equality depend on the manifest DIGEST (so two tags are two Features, not one declared twice), §Feature authorship states that "a single Feature may be installed more than once", and §Definition: Round Stable Sort supplies the tie-break — "Compare and sort each Feature from oldest to newest tag" — that the rejection's rationale claimed did not exist. Oracle 0.87.0 accepts the document and `features resolve-dependencies` returns BOTH digests, oldest tag first. Each entry carries a real option value rather than `{}` so the assertion can actually fail: a subset naming two keys whose expected value is `{}` matches any object at those keys, and one that named only the keys would still pass for a deacon that echoed the document and then installed one Feature. What that latter failure looks like is why this case is not the whole guard — see `case-readconfig-duplicate-feature-install-order-differential` for the resolved order and the Docker-backed install test in `crates/deacon/tests/integration_up_duplicate_features.rs` for both `install.sh` runs landing in the image. The retired wvr-features-duplicate-in-one-document is deliberately not replaced: it waived a divergence deacon was on the wrong side of.

The agreement half of #430, and the reason the fix is not just "deacon stopped erroring": before it, deacon exited 1 on a document the reference reads without comment, so this comparison could not have been written. It now compares deacon's resolved configuration to the reference's over the whole structured document — which includes the `features` map's KEY ORDER, since `preserve_order` keeps both sides' object order — so a deacon that silently dropped, reordered or de-duplicated one of the two entries diverges here rather than passing a subset assertion that only looked for their presence. #423's point applies: a record whose only evidence never runs the reference proves nothing about parity, and until this case existed the duplicate-Features behavior had exactly that.

The ORDER half of #430. `feature-dependencies.md` §Definition: Round Stable Sort sorts a round by resource name and then, "if the comparison is equal", from "oldest to newest tag" — the one rule in the document written for a `features` map that names one Feature twice. The fixture declares `:1.3.2` BEFORE `:1.3.1` for that reason: declaration order and tag order disagree, so an implementation that emitted the map's order would resolve them backwards and be caught. Measured against oracle 0.87.0 on 2026-08-03, `devcontainer features resolve-dependencies` returns `git@sha256:6d953e8c…` (which is `:1.3.1`) then `git@sha256:63c96e8a…` (`:1.3.2`) — oldest first, against the document's order. The comparison is the assertion here rather than a `jsonSubset` naming the two ids in sequence, because `compare.rs::is_json_subset` matches array elements ORDER-INSENSITIVELY: a subset listing them in the right order also passes for output listing them in the wrong one, which is the vacuous-assertion trap. `diff_paths` compares `featureSets` wholesale, so a reordering IS a divergence.

Covers the high-risk triple `hrt-readconfig-extends-chain-compose-declared-order`: a chain whose BASE link declares the Compose project and whose CHILD adds a declared-order Feature set. An operation runs with the workspace as its cwd, so naming only `--config` here is the reference's `--config`-alone invocation: the workspace is the cwd, and the reported folder is `/workspaces/<basename(cwd)>`. deacon used to re-anchor it at the config file's PARENT — which for the standard layout is `.devcontainer`, so this same case reported `/workspaces/.devcontainer` before #660 was fixed. `--mount-workspace-git-root false` is load-bearing for the ASSERTION, not for the claim: a hermetic case runs against the fixture directory in place, which lives inside this repository, so the default git-root walk would report the checkout's own root and make the expected string depend on where deacon was cloned. With the walk off, the cwd's basename is the answer and the normalizer's `<WORKSPACE_NAME>` token pins it. The anchor is not confined to this block: it also feeds `${localWorkspaceFolder}` and local feature-path resolution, which is why the fix was a ruling first. The symlink half of the same question (#665) is not expressible as a case — `copy_tree` cannot stage a symlinked directory into an isolated workspace — so it is carried by `integration_up_symlinked_workspace` and one hermetic `read-configuration` test.

Colons are separators all the way down: `${localEnv:NAME:default:a:b:c}` falls back to `default`, and everything past it is DISCARDED. deacon split the lookup body on the FIRST colon only and folded the rest into the default, so this fixture reported `[default:a:b:c]` before [#668](https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/668).

The reference splits the whole token on `:`, treats `parts[0]` as the variable name and `parts[1..]` as arguments, and `lookupValue` reads only `args[0]` and `args[1]` (`spec-common/variableSubstitution.ts:85-89` and `:137-155`). It has an explicit test for this exact shape at `src/test/variableSubstitution.test.ts:122`.

**The spec is the reason this is deacon's difference rather than a coin flip.** It documents no `:default` suffix at all — `${localEnv:VARIABLE_NAME}`, *"Unset variables are left blank"*, is the whole of it (`devcontainerjson-reference.md:155`). Defaults are a reference-CLI extension, so on this surface the reference is the authority by the standing rule and there is no second answer to weigh.

FOUR of the five keys are control arms, and they are what stop a wrong fix from passing: `SINGLE` pins that a single-segment default still works, `NONE` that a missing variable with no default is still the empty string, `EMPTY_NAME` that `${localEnv:}` — which reaches the same code with an empty name — is empty rather than an error, and `MULTI_ALIAS` that the `${env:*}` alias resolves through the identical rule. A fix that simply dropped everything after the first colon, or that stopped honouring defaults, fails on one of them.

`DEACON_PARITY_NO_SUCH_VAR` is never set by the harness or by CI, which is what makes the default the observable; a run in an environment that defined it would report the value and fail loudly rather than pass vacuously.

An authored `workspaceFolder` that is ITSELF a template seeds `${containerWorkspaceFolder}` with its RESOLVED value. deacon refused to seed any value containing `${` — a deliberate guard, with a comment saying so, in both the shared loader and `read-configuration` — so the token survived as a literal for exactly the common idiom `"workspaceFolder": "/workspaces/${localWorkspaceFolderBasename}"` ([#669](https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/669)).

The reference resolves that one value in `substitute()`'s prologue, before it substitutes the document (`spec-common/variableSubstitution.ts:30-32`), and tests the shape at `src/test/variableSubstitution.test.ts:60`.

**`workspaceFolder` is asserted alongside the two probes on purpose, and it is the sharp part of the case.** That field was substituted correctly BEFORE the fix as well — the defect was never in the document, it was in the CONTEXT built from it. Asserting the resolved field and the two tokens together is what says the two agree; a case that asserted only `workspaceFolder` would have been green throughout.

The two neighbouring shapes are NOT in this fixture and are carried by hermetic tests instead (`the_untemplated_workspace_folder_shapes_are_unchanged`): a literal `workspaceFolder` is seeded verbatim, and an unauthored one falls back to the container-side default `/workspaces/<basename>`. Both already matched the reference, measured at 0.87.0, and both must keep matching — without them, "seed whatever is authored" and "always use the default" would each pass this case.

Written in POST-NORMALIZATION vocabulary: `<WORKSPACE_NAME>` is the normalizer's token for the workspace basename, which is what `${localWorkspaceFolderBasename}` resolves to and therefore appears inside `/baz/…` here rather than only in a `/workspaces/…` path. That token reaches `chan-structured-output` because #636's case brought it there.

`${localEnv}` with NO variable name — and its `${env}` and `${containerEnv}` siblings — is left LITERAL, and `read-configuration` exits 0. **This case pins deacon's own answer, because the reference has no usable one to match.**

MEASURED at oracle 0.87.0 on this fixture: the reference exits **1** and prints NOTHING to stdout, and nothing to stderr beyond its version banner. Its `lookupValue` throws a `ContainerError` whose message would read *"'${localEnv}' in devcontainer.json can not be resolved because no environment variable name is given"* (`spec-common/variableSubstitution.ts:156-158`), but on this path the message never reaches the caller — so what a user actually gets is a silent exit 1 on a whole configuration because one token in it was malformed.

**DOCUMENTED CHOICE rather than a nonconformance, and the standing spec-silent rule is why the distinction has to be stated.** That rule — on a surface the spec does not describe, the reference is the authority — presupposes the reference produces an observable answer. A silent non-zero exit is a failure mode, not a behavior to conform to, and the spec describes neither this token nor any diagnostic for it. deacon's answer falls out of a rule it already has and applies everywhere else: an unrecognised variable is left unchanged (the module's documented workflow step 5, and the same answer this suite pins for `${notAVariable}`). `${localEnv}` names no variable, so it is not a variable reference.
